stem: Riya ties two identical stones to equal-length threads on her balcony hook. She pulls one aside by 5° and the other by 10° (both small angles) and releases them together. Which stone comes back to its starting point first?

options.A: The 10° stone, because it moves faster
options.B: The 5° stone, because its path is shorter
options.C: Both come back at the same time
options.D: It depends on which stone is slightly heavier

r1.text: The 10° one has more distance to go, so it needs more time.

r2.text: The 10° one goes farther but also moves faster, and these balance out, so the time is the same.

r3.text: The 10° one starts higher so it rushes down faster and gets back first.

stem: In the school lab, Neha's simple pendulum is 1.0 m long and swings with an amplitude of 4°. She restarts it with an amplitude of 8° (still a small angle). Take g = π² m/s². What is the period now?

r1.text: Double the swing means double the path, so the time doubles too.

r2.text: A wider swing gives more speed at the bottom, so it gets back sooner.

r3.text: The formula only has L and g, amplitude isn't in it, so the period doesn't change.

calc: T = 2π√(L/g) = 2π√(1.0/π²) = 2π/π = 2.0 s (same for 4° and 8°); SLIP C: 2π(L/g) without the root = 2/π ≈ 0.64 s

stem: Dadi's old pendulum wall clock in Pune is running down, so its pendulum's swing keeps getting smaller (always a small angle). What happens to the time taken for each swing?

options.A: It stays the same
options.B: It gets shorter, so the clock runs fast
options.C: It gets longer, so the clock runs slow
options.D: It depends on how heavy the brass bob is

r1.text: A smaller swing covers less distance but also moves slower, so each swing takes the same time.

r2.text: A smaller swing has less to travel, so it finishes quicker.

r3.text: A smaller swing moves slower, so it takes longer to finish.

verify_flags: Real clocks have a tiny amplitude-dependent (circular) error beyond small angles; ignored here as NCERT treats small-angle period as amplitude-independent.

stem: Ramesh, a mason, checks a wall with a 100 g plumb bob on a 0.25 m string; it swings gently (small angle). He swaps it for a 400 g bob on the same string. Take g = π² m/s². What is the new period?

r1.text: The heavier bob gets pulled down harder, so it swings back quicker.

r2.text: More mass means more pull but also more to move, so it cancels; only length and g matter.

r3.text: Four times the mass is harder to move, so it swings slower, like a heavier load on a spring.

verify_flags: Treats plumb bob as a point mass on a light string (simple pendulum).

stem: On a smooth lab table, Riya pulls a 0.5 kg block attached to a spring (k = 50 N/m) 0.1 m from its mean position and releases it. At that extreme point, which set of values is correct?

options.A: v = 0, a = 0, total energy = 0.25 J
options.B: v = 0, a = 10 m/s², total energy = 0.25 J
options.C: v = 0, a = 1 m/s², total energy = 0.25 J
options.D: v = 0, a = 10 m/s², total energy = 0 J

r1.text: At the end the block stops, so it has no energy at that moment. The energy comes back when it starts moving again.

r2.text: At the end the speed is zero, but the spring is stretched the most, so the pull and the acceleration are the biggest. All the energy is stored in the spring, so the total is still ½kA².

r3.text: The block is not moving at the end, so there is nothing changing, so the acceleration must be zero there.

stem: Meera swings on a jhoola in small arcs, close to SHM, with no air drag. At the highest point she stops for an instant. Which statement about that instant is correct?

options.A: Her acceleration is zero because she has stopped.
options.B: Her total energy is less than at the bottom because she is not moving.
options.C: Her acceleration is at its largest, pointing back toward the lowest point, and her total energy is the same as at the bottom.
options.D: Her acceleration is at its largest, and her total energy is also at its largest because she is highest.

r1.text: She is not moving at the top, so nothing is pushing her speed up or down. So no acceleration.

r2.text: At the top she has no speed, so she lost her kinetic energy. So the total energy has gone down at that point.

r3.text: At the top she is furthest from the middle, so the pull back is strongest. The kinetic energy just turned into potential energy, so the total did not change.

verify_flags: Swing treated as a small-angle simple pendulum; at the extreme the acceleration is tangential (g sinθ) toward the mean, with zero centripetal part since v = 0.

stem: Kabir's 2 kg toy cart, held between two springs on a smooth track, moves as x = 0.05 sin(4t) m. When the cart is at x = 0.05 m, what are its acceleration and total energy?

options.B: a = 0.8 m/s², E = 0 J
options.C: a = 0.8 m/s², E = 0.04 J now, but it rises to 0.08 J at the mean position

r1.text: x = 0.05 m is the end of the motion, so speed is zero but acceleration is ω²A, the biggest. Energy just moves between KE and PE, so the total stays ½mω²A².

r2.text: The cart stops at x = 0.05 m, so its acceleration is zero there.

r3.text: The cart is stopped at the end, so its energy is low there. It gets more energy when it zooms through the middle.

stem: In Shreya's college lab, water in a U-tube is disturbed and its level goes up and down in SHM. Assume no friction or viscosity. Which statement about the water column is correct?

options.A: When the level is highest, the column is at rest for an instant, but its acceleration is the largest.
options.B: When the level is highest, the column is at rest, so the net force on it is zero.
options.C: The total energy of the column is largest when it rushes through the mean level.
options.D: The column moves fastest when the level is highest.

r1.text: At the highest level the water stops, and when something stops there is no force on it.

r2.text: When the water is moving fastest it has the most energy, so total energy is biggest at the middle.

r3.text: At the highest level the water is furthest from the middle, so the restoring push is biggest, even though it is stopped for a moment.

verify_flags: Ideal U-tube (no viscosity) treated as SHM, restoring force from the level difference; check students know this setup from NCERT.

stem: Meera shakes one end of a long, tight rope 2 times per second, and the wave moves along at 6 m/s. Keeping the same rope and tension, she now shakes it 4 times per second. What happens?

options.A: The wave now travels at 12 m/s
options.B: The speed stays 6 m/s and the wavelength becomes 1.5 m
options.C: The speed stays 6 m/s and the wavelength becomes 6 m
options.D: The rope pieces get carried forward quicker, so the wave goes faster

r1.text: She is shaking it faster, so the wave also has to move faster.

r2.text: Same rope, same tension, so same speed. Only the waves get shorter because she shakes more often.

r3.text: Faster shaking pushes the rope itself forward quicker, and the wave rides along with it.

calc: v = √(T/μ) unchanged = 6 m/s; λ = v/f = 6/4 = 1.5 m (earlier 6/2 = 3 m)
verify_flags: Assumes ideal uniform string; the 6 m/s value is given, T and μ not stated

stem: At a Diwali mela, a flute player plays a 500 Hz note and a 1000 Hz note at the same instant. Priya stands 343 m away. Take the speed of sound in air as 343 m/s. Which note reaches her first?

options.A: The 1000 Hz note, because faster vibration means faster sound
options.B: Whichever note is played louder
options.C: Both reach her together, after about 1 s
options.D: Neither, until the puff of air from the flute blows across to her

r1.text: Sound speed depends on the air, not on the note, so both take the same time.

r2.text: The high note vibrates more times every second, so it must travel quicker.

r3.text: A louder note has more push behind it, so it gets there first.

calc: t = d/v = 343/343 = 1 s for both notes
verify_flags: Uses 343 m/s for air at about 20 °C; NCERT also quotes 331 m/s at 0 °C

stem: On sports day, Ravi and Anil each send one pulse along identical ropes tied to a post, with equal tension. Ravi jerks his hand much higher and much quicker than Anil. Whose pulse reaches the post first?

options.A: Ravi's, because his pulse is taller
options.B: Ravi's, because he moved his hand quicker
options.C: Ravi's, because his rope gets dragged towards the post more
options.D: Both pulses reach the post at the same time

r1.text: A big jerk pulls the rope along towards the post, so the pulse arrives sooner.

r2.text: A taller pulse carries more energy, so it runs faster.

r3.text: The ropes and tension are the same, so the pulse speed is the same, no matter how he jerks.

verify_flags: Treats pulses as linear; a very large jerk can slightly raise tension, ignored here

stem: At Nagpur station, a worker taps a long steel rail with a hammer. Children 1 km down the line, with an ear on the rail, hear the tap. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Each bit of steel only vibrates about its own place; the disturbance travels to the children
options.B: Bits of steel are pushed along the rail until they reach the children
options.C: Hitting the rail harder would make the sound reach them sooner
options.D: Tapping more times each second would make the sound reach them sooner

r1.text: A harder hit gives the sound a stronger push, so it travels faster.

r2.text: The steel stays where it is and just vibrates; only the vibration passes along.

r3.text: The hammer shoves the steel forward, and that moving steel carries the sound to them.

verify_flags: Sound in steel is both longitudinal and transverse; statement A kept general on purpose

stem: Priya tunes her sitar string against a 440 Hz tuning fork. Sounding both together, she hears the loudness throb. If the string is at 444 Hz, how many beats per second does she hear?

options.A: 884 beats per second
options.B: 442 beats per second
options.C: 4 beats per second
options.D: 8 beats per second

r1.text: Both sounds are playing together, so I just add the two frequencies.

r2.text: The beat should be the middle value, halfway between 440 and 444.

r3.text: The two sounds drift in and out of step, and that happens as many times per second as their difference.

stem: In the school band, two flutes play notes of 512 Hz and 506 Hz together. Rohan hears the sound swell and fade. Which best describes what he hears?

options.A: A tone of about 509 Hz whose loudness swells 6 times per second
options.B: A tone whose loudness swells 1018 times per second
options.C: A tone whose loudness swells 509 times per second
options.D: Loudness swells 6 times per second, and sound energy is destroyed in each quiet moment

r1.text: When it goes quiet the two waves have cancelled, so that bit of energy is just gone.

r2.text: The swelling happens at the difference, 6 times a second, and the note I hear is about the average.

r3.text: Two flutes are playing at once, so the swells come at both frequencies added up.

calc: f_beat = 512 Hz - 506 Hz = 6 Hz; heard pitch = (512 + 506)/2 = 509 Hz
verify_flags: Heard pitch = average holds only approximately, for close frequencies; in quiet moments energy is redistributed in space/time, not destroyed

stem: At an evening bhajan, the two reeds playing one harmonium note are slightly off: 349 Hz and 352 Hz. Arjun hears the note throb. How many throbs per second does he hear?

options.A: 701 throbs per second
options.B: 350.5 throbs per second
options.C: 0, because the two sounds cancel and the note dies out
options.D: 3 throbs per second

r1.text: The throbbing comes from the two reeds going in and out of step, which is 352 minus 349 times a second.

r2.text: The throb should be at the average of the two reeds, somewhere in the middle.

r3.text: Both reeds sound together, so the throbs are the two frequencies added.

verify_flags: Harmonium reed frequencies are illustrative, not real tuning values

stem: On sports day, Sana and Dev flick opposite ends of a long tug-of-war rope at the same instant. Sana's pulse is upward, Dev's is an equal downward one. They meet and the rope looks flat for a moment. What happens next?

options.A: Both pulses are gone for good; their energy was used up in cancelling
options.B: Sana's pulse carries on toward Dev and Dev's carries on toward Sana, both unchanged
options.C: The pulses rebound, so Sana's upward pulse heads back toward Sana
options.D: The pulses rebound and return smaller, as some energy is lost in the collision

r1.text: They hit each other in the middle and bounce back, like two balls.

r2.text: Up plus down makes zero, so after that the pulses are finished.

r3.text: They only add while overlapping; after that each pulse keeps going as if nothing happened.

verify_flags: Assumes an ideal rope with negligible damping; real rope pulses shrink slowly from friction, not from meeting

stem: Arjun is 1.6 m tall. He wants a plane mirror on his bedroom wall, hung at the right height, in which he can see himself from head to toe. What is the shortest mirror that will work?

options.C: Less than 0.8 m, if he stands far enough back

r1.text: If he stands farther away, more of him fits in, so a smaller mirror is enough.

r2.text: Light from his feet bounces off the mirror halfway down to his eyes, so he only needs half his height, wherever he stands.

r3.text: The image is on the glass, so the glass has to be as tall as he is.

verify_flags: Assumes a vertical plane mirror with its top edge midway between Arjun's eyes and the top of his head.

stem: At a salon in Pune, Meera sees only her face down to her shoulders in a small mirror fixed on the wall. She takes two steps back. What part of herself does she see now?

options.A: More of herself, down to her waist
options.B: Less of herself, only her face
options.C: Still only her face down to her shoulders
options.D: Her whole body, if she goes back far enough

r1.text: Farther from the mirror means a wider view, so more of her fits in.

r2.text: Her image stays on the glass while she backs away, so the glass covers more of her.

r3.text: Her image moves back as much as she does, so the mirror still covers the same part of her.

verify_flags: Assumes the mirror stays fixed and Meera's eye height does not change as she steps back.

stem: Kabir, 1.7 m tall, is buying a mirror for his hostel room in Vellore. He will stand about 3 m from it. What is the shortest mirror, hung at the right height, that shows him head to toe?

options.B: Less than 0.85 m, because standing 3 m back means he needs less mirror
options.C: 0.85 m only if he stands close; at 3 m he needs a longer one

r1.text: He needs half his height, and the distance doesn't matter because his image moves back with him.

r2.text: His image sits on the mirror, so the mirror must be his full height.

r3.text: Standing far back lets more of him fit, so a shorter mirror will do.

verify_flags: Assumes a vertical plane mirror with its top edge midway between Kabir's eyes and the top of his head.

stem: Ananya stands 3 m in front of the big wall mirror in her dance class. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Her image is 3 m behind the mirror, so it is 6 m from her
options.B: Her image is on the mirror surface, so it is 3 m from her
options.C: If she moves back to 5 m, she will see more of her body in the same mirror
options.D: Her image is 3 m behind the mirror, so it is 3 m from her

r1.text: What I see is right on the glass, so the image is just 3 m away.

r2.text: The image is as far behind the mirror as she is in front, so 3 m + 3 m = 6 m.

r3.text: Moving back lets the mirror catch more of her body.

stem: Meera points a waterproof torch up from inside a fish tank. The beam hits the water surface at 30° to the normal (water n = 4/3). What does the beam do at the surface?

options.A: It comes out into the air bending toward the normal
options.B: It comes out into the air bending away from the normal
options.C: It is totally reflected back into the water
options.D: It comes out into the air without bending at all

r1.text: Light always bends toward the normal when it goes into a new medium.

r2.text: Water to air means going into a rarer medium, so it bends away, and 30° is less than the critical angle so it still gets out.

r3.text: Light hitting a water surface from below just reflects back fully, the angle doesn't really matter.

stem: Inside Rohan's glass paperweight (n = 1.5), a laser beam reaches the flat top face at 25° to the normal. What happens as the beam passes out into the room air?

options.A: It is totally reflected back into the paperweight
options.B: It bends toward the normal, leaving at less than 25°
options.C: It bends away from the normal, leaving at more than 25°
options.D: It goes straight out because glass and air are both transparent

r1.text: Any time light crosses glass, it bends toward the normal, that's the rule.

r2.text: Light inside glass can always get trapped by total reflection at the surface.

r3.text: Glass to air is dense to rare, so it bends away, and 25° is below 41.8° so it comes out.

stem: A lamp fixed at the bottom of a hotel swimming pool sends a ray up to the water surface at 40° to the normal (water n = 4/3). What happens to this ray?

options.A: It enters the air at about 28.8° from the normal
options.B: It is totally reflected back into the pool
options.C: It enters the air at about 53.3° from the normal
options.D: It enters the air at about 59.0° from the normal

r1.text: Water to air it bends away, so n sin 40° gives sin r = 0.857, about 59°, and 40° is under the critical angle.

r2.text: Underwater light hitting the top just bounces back fully, the pool surface acts like a mirror.

r3.text: It should bend toward the normal, so the angle in air must come out smaller than 40°.

verify_flags: A uses sin r = (3/4) sin 40° = 0.482 -> 28.8° (bending toward normal); C is the slip of multiplying the angle, 40° × 4/3 ≈ 53.3°; 40° < C ≈ 48.6° so no TIR

stem: At a science fair, Kavya shines a laser from air onto a glass block (n = 1.5) at 60° to the normal, which is more than glass's critical angle of 41.8°. What happens at the surface?

options.A: The beam enters the glass, bending toward the normal to about 35°
options.B: Total internal reflection, because 60° is bigger than 41.8°
options.C: The beam enters the glass without bending at all
options.D: All the light reflects back into the air, as the glass acts like a mirror at large angles

r1.text: Once the angle crosses the critical angle, total internal reflection happens, whichever side the light comes from.

r2.text: Total reflection needs light going from glass to air; here it is air to glass, so it just refracts in and bends toward the normal.

r3.text: Light bends toward the normal at every surface, so it goes in bent toward the normal.

verify_flags: Some light is always partially reflected at the surface; option D says ALL light reflects, which is the wrong part. r3 (R3) reaches the right answer for the wrong reason, by design

stem: Riya keeps a candle 30 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. She takes away the screen and sticks black paper over the top half of the lens. What happens to the image?

options.A: Only half of the candle's image forms, 60 cm behind the lens
options.B: The full image still forms 60 cm behind the lens, only dimmer
options.C: No image forms anywhere, because there is no screen
options.D: The full image forms 12 cm behind the lens, only dimmer

r1.text: Without a screen there is nothing to hold the image, so it doesn't form.

r2.text: Every point of the candle still sends light through the open half, and those rays still meet at 60 cm.

r3.text: The paper blocks the top half of the lens, so that part of the picture is lost.

verify_flags: D uses the sign slip 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12, giving 12 cm

stem: Arjun's magnifying glass makes a sharp image of the ceiling tubelight on his notebook. A friend's thumb covers the left half of the lens, and Arjun slides the notebook away. What about the image now?

options.A: It vanishes, because the notebook was what made it
options.B: Half of the tubelight's image is missing, at the same spot
options.C: It moves along with the notebook to the new place
options.D: A complete but dimmer image still forms in the air at the same spot

r1.text: Light from every part of the tubelight still goes through the open half and meets at the same spot, page or no page.

r2.text: The thumb blocks half the lens, so half the image goes dark.

r3.text: The image was only on the paper. Take the paper away and it's gone.

verify_flags: Assumes the tubelight is far enough that the image forms near the focus on the same side as the notebook

stem: In the lab, Meera puts a bulb 15 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Tape covers the lower half of the lens, and there is no screen on the bench. What is true about the image?

options.A: Only the top half of the image forms, 30 cm from the lens
options.B: No image forms until a screen is placed 30 cm from the lens
options.C: A full, inverted, dimmer image forms 30 cm from the lens, twice the bulb's size
options.D: A full, dimmer image forms 6 cm from the lens

r1.text: Tape on the bottom half means the bottom half of the lens can't make its part of the picture.

r2.text: The light needs a screen to land on, otherwise there's no image yet.

r3.text: Rays from each point of the bulb still pass through the top half and cross at 30 cm, screen or not.

verify_flags: D uses the sign slip 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6, giving 6 cm

stem: At a science fair, a big convex lens forms a real image of a diya in mid-air; there is no screen. A price sticker covers half the lens. Kabir stands well beyond the image and looks back at the lens. What does he see?

options.A: The whole diya, upside down and a little dimmer
options.B: Nothing, since a real image needs a screen to show up
options.C: Only half the diya, because the sticker blocks the rest
options.D: The diya upright and enlarged, like through a magnifying glass

r1.text: The sticker stops light from that half of the lens, so that half of the diya can't reach his eyes.

r2.text: The rays really meet at the image spot and then carry on to his eyes, and each point still gets light through the free half.

r3.text: There's no screen, so the light never forms a picture he can look at.

verify_flags: Assumes Kabir's eye is at least about 25 cm beyond the image and inside the cone of rays leaving it; if the cone misses his eye he sees only the lens lit up

stem: Riya sets up a double slit with a red laser in her college lab. Keeping the laser and screen fixed, she swaps in slits that are half as far apart. What happens to the fringes?

options.A: They become half as wide
options.B: They become twice as wide
options.C: Same width, but brighter, because closer slits make extra light energy
options.D: Same width; only the colour of the fringes changes

r1.text: Slits closer means the whole pattern squeezes, so the fringes get thinner.

r2.text: Fringe width is lambda D by d, so if d is halved the width doubles.

r3.text: When the slits are closer the beams overlap more and interference makes more light.

stem: In his school lab, Arjun uses a 600 nm laser, a screen 1.5 m away and slits 0.30 mm apart, getting 3.0 mm fringes. He swaps in slits 0.15 mm apart, keeping everything else same. New fringe width?

options.A: 1.5 mm
options.C: 6.0 mm
options.D: 3.0 mm, but the bright fringes get brighter because closer slits make extra light

r1.text: Beta equals lambda D over d, and d got halved, so beta doubles to 6 mm.

r2.text: Half the slit gap means half the fringe gap, so 1.5 mm.

r3.text: Width won't change, the interference just puts more energy into the bright bands.

verify_flags: SLIP option B (0.60 mm) is a power-of-ten slip on 6.0 mm

stem: At a science fair in Pune, Kabir's double-slit fringes are too thin to see clearly. Without changing the laser or moving the screen, what should he do to make the fringes wider?

options.A: Use slits that are farther apart
options.B: Cover one slit, so the half pattern left spreads out wider
options.C: Use a stronger laser so interference adds more light to each fringe
options.D: Use slits that are closer together

r1.text: If one slit is blocked you only get half the fringes, so they have more room.

r2.text: Slits farther apart spread everything out, so the fringes get wider too.

r3.text: Fringe width goes as 1 by d, so a smaller slit gap gives wider fringes.

verify_flags: Assumes slit width and wavelength unchanged; a stronger laser changes brightness only, not fringe width

stem: During a power cut, Meera shines a battery laser through a double slit in her Chennai hostel and sees clear fringes on the wall. Her friend sticks tape over one slit. What does the wall show now?

options.A: The fringes vanish; a broad, dimmer patch of light from the open slit remains
options.B: Only the half of the fringe pattern on the open slit's side remains
options.C: The wall goes almost dark, since the light was being produced by the two beams interfering
options.D: Every second bright fringe disappears, leaving half the fringes

r1.text: The bright light came from interference, so without it there is hardly any light.

r2.text: Fringes need waves from both slits to meet, so with one slit there are no fringes, just its own spread-out light.

r3.text: Each slit makes its own share of fringes, so one slit leaves half of them.

verify_flags: Open slit gives its single-slit diffraction pattern: broad central band, centre intensity I0 instead of 4I0; looks uniform-ish only if slit is narrow

stem: In the school lab, Kavya makes a single slit narrower. Then she slides a third polaroid at 45° between two crossed polaroids lit by unpolarised light of intensity I0. What does she observe?

options.A: Central maximum gets narrower; I0/8 gets through the polaroids
options.B: Central maximum gets wider; no light gets through the polaroids
options.C: Central maximum gets wider; I0/8 gets through the polaroids
options.D: Central maximum gets wider; I0/4 gets through the polaroids

r1.text: A polaroid only blocks light, so putting one more in can't make the dark side bright.

r2.text: A thin slit spreads light more because width is 2λD/a, and the middle polaroid turns the light so some passes both.

r3.text: Less gap squeezes the light, so the bright band also gets thinner.

calc: Width = 2λD/a rises as a falls; I = (I0/2)·cos²45°·cos²45° = (I0/2)(1/2)(1/2) = I0/8
verify_flags: Ideal polaroids assumed (no absorption beyond Malus's law)
Option D slip = cos instead of cos²: (I0/2)·cos45°·cos45° = I0/4

stem: At a Pune science fair, Rohan narrows a razor-blade slit in front of a laser pointer. His friend Sana slips a polaroid at 45° between two crossed polaroids taped over a torch. What changes?

options.A: Laser's central bright patch shrinks; torch side lights up a little
options.B: Central bright patch spreads out; torch side lights up a little
options.C: Central bright patch spreads out; torch side stays dark
options.D: Central bright patch vanishes; torch becomes as bright as with no sheets

r1.text: Smaller gap means smaller patch, the light just comes out thinner.

r2.text: The crossed sheets already block everything, and a sheet can only block more.

r3.text: The narrow slit bends light out more, and the tilted sheet turns the light so part of it gets past the last sheet.

stem: Ananya's single slit (λ = 600 nm, screen 1.5 m away, a = 0.12 mm) gives a 15 mm central band. She narrows it to a = 0.06 mm and slips a 45° polaroid between two crossed ones. Which is right?

options.A: Central band 7.5 mm; one-eighth of the incoming unpolarised light now passes
options.B: Central band 30 mm; the crossed pair still passes no light
options.C: Central band 30 mm; one-quarter of the incoming unpolarised light now passes
options.D: Central band 30 mm; one-eighth of the incoming unpolarised light now passes

r1.text: Width is 2λD/a so halving a doubles it to 30 mm, and half, then half, then half again gives one-eighth.

r2.text: Half the slit, half the band, so 15 becomes 7.5 mm.

r3.text: Crossed means zero, and adding a sheet can't bring light back.

verify_flags: Check: 2(600e-9)(1.5)/(0.12e-3) = 0.015 m = 15 mm for the original slit

stem: At a Kochi exhibition, Neha narrows a slit in front of a laser. She also holds two polaroid sunglass lenses crossed in 64 W/m² of sunlight and slides a third lens at 45° between them. What does she find?

options.A: Laser's central band widens; 8 W/m² gets through the lenses
options.B: Laser's central band narrows; 8 W/m² gets through the lenses
options.C: Laser's central band widens; still 0 W/m² gets through the lenses
options.D: Laser's central band widens; 16 W/m² gets through the lenses

r1.text: Thin slit bends light more so the band widens, and 64 halves to 32, then ×½ and ×½ at the two 45° turns gives 8.

r2.text: A narrower slit lets through a narrower beam, so the band on the wall shrinks.

r3.text: Lenses are filters, a third one can only cut more light, so it stays zero.

calc: I = (64/2)·cos²45°·cos²45° = 32 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 8 W/m²; width 2λD/a grows as a shrinks
